reasoning: This is a pass. The line moved 3 points through the key number 7, and the lessons say to treat a moved number as fair. Virginia's pass defense and SMU's weak run defense point one way, and Virginia's 0-2 road record, travel and SMU's bye point the other. The [angle] that stood out was SMU's bye against Virginia's Friday travel for an 11 a.m. local kickoff. A clear Hillman/Agard secondary collapse would have moved me toward SMU.

The deciding factor was the market. The line fell from 4 to 3.5 and Indiana's moneyline shortened despite about 80% of tickets and nearly all the money on Ohio State, which is reverse line movement toward the underdog, the one market sign that has held up. The [angle] that stood out was Ohio State's patched-together right side of the line facing the Big Ten's best pass rush. I shaded my projection back toward the line (Ohio State by about 1.5), so this is a lean, not strong. A move to Ohio State -4.5 or confirmation that Siereveld was back would have made it a pass.

This is a pass. The efficiency gap (SP+ about 17) says Northwestern by double digits, but the market moved from -9.5 to -7 on Michigan State money, and the lessons say not to fight the line with ratings everyone has. The surprising [angle] was Fitzgerald's first game against the program he built, with his former coordinator on the other sideline, together with Northwestern's poor Big Ten road form. Shaded back toward the line, my projection lands within about 2 points of the key number 7, so I passed. A line back at 9+ or confirmed Michigan State defensive absences would have tipped it.

This is a pass. Texas's elite defense against Florida's collapsing defense argues for a margin around the models' 14-17, but Texas's offense has won every Power Four game by 3 or fewer, and the number already moved 2 points toward Texas to 11.5. The [angle] that stood out was Texas going 0-for-3 at pulling away from good teams despite its defense. Shaded halfway back to the line, my projection sits about a point from the spread. A clear injury to a Florida offensive starter or Florida's QB would have pushed it toward Texas.

This is a pass. The line moved from 10.5 to 14 on Mississippi State's QB injury, so the lessons say to treat 14 as fair and not re-count Taylor's foot as a reason for LSU. His status was still unresolved on game morning and decides the game, which is itself a pass trigger. The [angle] that stood out was a top-5 EPA offense whose pass-first plan runs straight into LSU's top-5 pass defense with a hobbled QB in gusty wind. A confirmed backup QB start without a further line move would have pushed me toward LSU.

The deciding factor was the market. Tech moved from -12.5 to -16.5 by game day, and SP+ plus home field (about 21) and Action Network (-18.5) sit above the slate's 14.5, so this side is 2 points better than the closing number rather than a bet into the moved line. Arizona State's 106th-ranked offense, which converts under 30% on third down, gives little backdoor path. The [angle] was revenge for Tech's only regular-season loss last year, coming off a bye. A Hammond-led turnover game is the risk; if the slate number had matched the -16.5 close, this would have been a pass.

SP+ (Alabama by 3.8) and Tennessee's defense point to Tennessee +7.5. Tennessee's broken passing game (128th in pass success, a 10.3 QBR from MacIntyre) and Alabama's top-10 run defense against Tennessee's one strength point the other way. Shading my projection halfway to the line gives about Alabama by 6.5, within 2 points of 7.5, so pass. The surprising angle is the QB uncertainty: Brandon was back at practice and Heupel wouldn't name a starter. A confirmed Brandon start, or the line reaching 9+, would have made Tennessee a lean.

The models (Dimers 35-15) and the market sit on top of the 19.5 line. Auburn's inability to score argues for Georgia, while Georgia's own modest scoring (20 points vs Alabama) and the letdown spot argue for Auburn, so this is a pass. The most interesting angle is the move toward Georgia against Auburn money, which LESSONS says not to follow. A clear Auburn QB or line injury would have tipped it to Georgia.

The deciding numbers are SP+ (nearly a pick'em) against a 5.5-point line, plus Missouri's elite run defense and turnover margin against an Ole Miss defense in the bottom third by EPA. Shading halfway toward the line still leaves Ole Miss by about 3, so Missouri +5.5 is a lean. The surprising angle is Austin Simmons, the former Ole Miss starter, returning to Oxford. Clear money moving the line to 6.5+ toward Ole Miss, or Missouri's bad red-zone offense, are why this isn't strong.

Miami's offensive efficiency, its returning defenders after a bye and FSU's road defense (47 PPG allowed) favor Miami. The rivalry's history of close margins and the rain favor FSU. The models and market sit right at 20.5-21.5, so this is a pass. The notable angle is FSU's 44-6 collapse after nearly leading Louisville 21-0. A confirmed Miami secondary return plus a line at 19 or lower would have made Miami a lean.

SP+ (4.4) and Dimers (4) both put this right on the 4.5 line. Houston's third-down and run-defense edges are offset by its leaky red zone and Oklahoma State's scoring streak in a game with a 62.5 total, so pass. The surprising angle is Oklahoma State's 91-newcomer rebuild under Eric Morris. A firm line at 3.5 or a confirmed Ridgle absence would have changed the calculus.

Notre Dame's efficiency profile and BYU's depleted backfield favor the Irish. But the line already moved through 10 on the Martin injury, and LESSONS says not to bet further in the direction of an injury move. Kalshi and Dimers both sit on the number, so pass. The most interesting angle is that this is Notre Dame's first ranked opponent and first hostile road night game. A line back at 9.5 would have made Notre Dame a lean.

The market already moved the number to a near pick'em after the Iamaleava injury, and the evidence splits: Wisconsin's elite pass defense against a backup QB vs. UCLA's strong run game and defense against a Wisconsin offense that can't run. My raw lean was Wisconsin by a point or so; shaded halfway back to the line it's UCLA by about 1, inside 2 points of -2.5, so I pass. The most interesting angle is UCLA's unrepeatable 7-takeaway game at Oregon inflating its form. Confirmation that Kawecki would miss would have pushed me further from Wisconsin.

Oklahoma has the better team and an elite defense, but its offense is among the worst in FBS by success rate. Game-day news then took away its top WR (Livingstone), its top CB (Bowen) and up to three offensive linemen, while Kentucky forces turnovers against a turnover-prone QB. My raw view was Oklahoma by about 3; shaded toward the line it's Oklahoma by 4, so Kentucky +6.5 covers by about 2.5. The decisive angle is the late Oklahoma injury report. Confirmation that Baxter would play would have strengthened this; an early Oklahoma lead with Kentucky's offense stalling on third down is the risk.

The models (SP+, two projections around Utah by 20) favor Utah, but the market has moved two to three points toward Colorado, and Colorado has a top-3 defense by adjusted EPA, a bye and a QB who knows Utah's staff. Colorado's offense can't score on good teams, though, which is the bar a 14.5-point underdog has to clear. Shaded to the moved line, I have Utah by about 13.5, within 2 points of the spread, so I pass. Confirmation that Scudero and Lester were both out would have nudged me toward Utah.

Wake has the far better offense and Cal's run defense and coordinator turmoil are real problems, but the line has already moved from -8.5 to -10 with the money, and the models land only one to three points past it (SP+ 13, Dimers 11). Shaded toward the line, I had Wake by about 11.5, a 1.5-point edge, with Cal's QB decision unresolved. That's inside my pass band. A confirmed Brousseau start, or an OC change that left Cal's offense in worse shape, would have made it a Wake lean.

Before I saw the result, the evidence was balanced. Seattle's top-ranked defense (yards per play) and Denver's missing secondary (Surtain and Hufanga out) were set against Seattle's short week at altitude, its thin backfield, Darnold's recent dip and wind and rain. My projection (SEA by about 2, shaded to the line) sat within a point of the 2.5/3 spread, so I'd pass. The most surprising [angle] was a short-week road favorite at altitude in bad weather with a total near 40. Getting Denver +3.5 or better, or Seattle at -1.5, would have made it a lean.

Jacksonville is the better team, is already settled in London, and has a top-three defense, but the market has already priced it at a fair -2.5/-3 and Houston's defense and the Jaguars' backup left tackle against Will Anderson keep this a one-score game. Shaded toward the line, my projection is Jaguars by about 2.5, inside the pass band at -3. The most surprising angle was the midweek Marvin Harrison Jr. trade. A clear Jaguars -2.5 or a Montgomery-plus-Collins absence would have pushed me to a lean.

The Hurts injury caused a roughly 5-point swing to Panthers -3.5, and the lessons say to treat a 3+ point injury move as fair and not to re-count the injury. My projection, Panthers by about 3.5, sits on the number. Carolina's bye and Philadelphia's London return favour the Panthers, while Carolina's two missing starting corners are the most surprising angle and keep McKee live. A -2.5 would have made Carolina a lean.

With Jackson out and Huntley starting, the market drifted from -4.5 to -3.5 and the total dropped, so the slate's -4.5 sits a point above the settled number. A Huntley-led, run-heavy Baltimore against a Browns defense that has been unbeaten at home projects to about a field goal. The most surprising angle was Cleveland's league-worst sack rate allowed meeting a possibly returning Hendrickson, which is the main risk. A confirmed Jackson start would have made this a pass.

Two QB injury stories, Williams returning and Penix's ribs, drove a roughly 4.5-point swing to Chicago -3. The lesson is to treat that number as fair, and the outcome hinges on Penix's late status, which I couldn't confirm cleanly. Atlanta's run game against Chicago's weak run defense, plus the Sweat suspension, argued Falcons, but Williams' return isn't in Chicago's recent numbers. Pass.

Every input points Rams, but the 12.5-point line already reflects Arizona's collapse, and the Rams are only 2-3. Shading the pundits' 14-18-point projections halfway back to the line gives about 13, inside the pass band. Arizona dealing Harrison midweek was the most surprising angle. A move to -11 with no news would have made the Rams a lean.

Buffalo is clearly better, but it's on a short week after a Monday overtime game, with a bye next, and its defense allows 28 a game. Money has drifted to Las Vegas against 65% of tickets, with the line off its open of 6. Shading Buffalo's edge back toward the line gives about 3.5, so +5.5 has a small cushion. The short-week, bye-next spot was the key angle. A return to -4.5 would have made it a pass.

On the numbers this is a mismatch: the worst offense in the league, a line of four rookies plus Alt out, against an unbeaten Chiefs team off a bye. That points to KC by 9-10. Shading halfway back to the 7.5 line gives about 8.5, within 2 points of the spread, and KC's recent wins have been close in a low-total game. The most surprising angle was that the line went to 8.5 and came back to 7.5 on game day even with the handle on KC. I would have taken KC if the Chargers' remaining receivers (McConkey) had been confirmed out with the line still at 7.5.

A near pick'em between two good offenses and a Dallas defense that is the league's worst against the pass, partly offset by GB's soft schedule of backup QBs and its thin secondary. The 3-point move toward GB came from one bad Dallas game rather than injury news; I treat the new number as fair and don't fade it. My projection of GB by about 1.5 sits on the line, so I pass. Most surprising angle: GB's good pass-defense numbers came against three backup QBs.

A pick'em after a 3-4 point swing toward New Orleans on Winston replacing Dart. Per lessons I treat the moved number as fair, and the reverse movement here favors the favorite, which hasn't been a reliable sign. Model and expert views are split, so I pass at about NO by 0.5. The most interesting angle was the Giants' fatigue after a 54-attempt OT game in the rain.

Power ratings say NE by about 11, but the market came down 3 points from -10 to -7 on the Patriots losing both starting corners and possibly their LT. Per lessons I treat the new number as fair and don't bet further in the move's direction. My shaded projection of NE by about 7.5 is on the number, so I pass. Most surprising angle: the Jets' 5th-ranked defense and 8-sack game against a NE line that may be missing its LT.

A low-total game with a backup QB for Tampa Bay. TB has the rest, the run game and the better defense by EPA, while Pittsburgh has the QB edge and Daniels carries interception risk. My shaded projection of PIT by about 1.5 is within 2 points of the 2.5 spread, so the pass trigger applies. The most interesting angle was TB's 10 days of rest vs PIT's travel on a normal week. A confirmed opener showing the line had come toward PIT on Mayfield's injury would have changed nothing, since that news is already priced.

The Titans' offense can't score (11.6 PPG, 187 yards last week), which argues against the big dog. But the Colts' defense is bad (6.2 yards per play allowed), and the line has already moved 3.5 points toward Indy, which per lessons I don't chase. A shaded projection of IND by about 7 sits on the number, so I pass. The surprising angle: the line rose after the Colts' loss, as if the market priced Tennessee's floor rather than Indy's form.

On efficiency the numbers clearly favor San Francisco: a top-2 offense against a bottom-10 pass defense that collapses late, plus a one-armed Daniels with no healthy backup. Models put it at about SF by 8. Against that, SF's receiving corps was gutted, and sharp money at Circa pushed the line from -8 to -7.5 against SF-heavy tickets. Shaded halfway to the line, my projection is about SF by 7, inside the 2-point pass band of -7.5. The most surprising [angle] was the sharp move toward a beat-up road dog with the league's worst second-half defense. A clean -6.5 or better would have made it a lean on SF; a 9+ would have made it a lean on Washington.
